title: Development against the odds
gist: The World Bank Group's latest Atlas of Global Development finds countries are progressing at their slowest average pace since 1950, with more than 50 developing economies on track to need a century or more to reach high-income development levels, and the slowdown began before the pandemic. Rwanda, the Kyrgyz Republic, Cambodia and Ethiopia are offered as counterexamples showing that state capacity, digital connectivity and pragmatic off-grid energy solutions still deliver rapid gains.

insights.claim: The World Bank Group's latest Atlas of Global Development shows that on average countries are progressing at their slowest pace since 1950, across poverty reduction, health, schooling, infrastructure and incomes.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A structural deceleration in emerging-market development undercuts the convergence assumption underlying long-horizon EM growth and consumption forecasts.
insights.locator: At the broadest level, the picture is sobering

insights.claim: If current trends persist, more than 50 developing economies could take a century or more just to reach the development levels currently seen in high-income countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Century-scale convergence timelines imply persistent labor-cost and demand gaps, reshaping expectations for frontier-market consumer markets.
insights.locator: This slowdown is visible across many of the measures

insights.claim: The development slowdown began before the pandemic, so recent shocks such as pandemic aftershocks, climate disasters, debt distress and conflict are aggravating factors rather than the root cause, which lies in weak productivity growth, insufficient investment, fragile institutions and policy frameworks favoring short-term firefighting over long-term transformation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: If the cause is structural rather than cyclical, post-shock recovery narratives are misplaced and the slowdown will persist without institutional reform.
insights.locator: It is tempting to attribute the slowdown entirely to recent shocks

insights.claim: Slower development directly translates into hundreds of millions of people waiting decades longer for better jobs, schools, health care and higher living standards.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Frames the slowdown as a demand-side loss for global markets, not only a humanitarian issue.

themes.theme: Rwanda: state capacity and structural change

insights.claim: Rwanda reduced extreme poverty from about 90 percent to less than 40 percent after the 1994 genocide and could bring it below 10 percent by 2050 if it sustains this pace.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: One of the largest documented poverty declines available, and a live test case for whether the trajectory holds through 2050.
insights.locator: What Successful Countries Have in Common

insights.claim: Rwanda's gains came from combining sustained growth with a capable state, large-scale public investment and a structural shift of labor into higher-productivity services such as trade, tourism, transport and conferences.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Services-led structural transformation, not manufacturing, drove this case, which challenges the standard industrialization pathway for low-income countries.

insights.claim: Growth alone is not enough for lasting progress, which depends on institutions able to implement reforms consistently over time.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Implementation capacity is the scarce input, so state-capacity indicators may predict development outcomes better than growth forecasts.
insights.quote: Lasting progress depends on institutions that can implement reforms consistently over time.
insights.locator: Rwanda's experience reminds us that growth alone is not enough

insights.claim: Digital infrastructure is becoming as fundamental to development as roads or electricity.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Reclassifies connectivity as core development infrastructure, which supports concessional financing and public investment flows into telecom.
insights.locator: Digital infrastructure is becoming as fundamental

insights.claim: Internet access in the Kyrgyz Republic rose from roughly 30 percent in 2015 to more than 90 percent in 2024 through state-led expansion of physical infrastructure, laying fiber-optic cable across underserved areas and strengthening cross-border connections.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that a fiber build-out model can triple penetration in under a decade, a template for landlocked economies and their equipment suppliers.
insights.locator: In the Kyrgyz Republic, internet access rose

insights.claim: Cambodia's internet access jumped from just 7 percent to around 70 percent using a market-driven model of rapid mobile phone adoption and strong private investment, leapfrogging fixed-line systems and moving directly to mobile broadband.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A tenfold penetration gain via private mobile investment shows the mobile-leapfrog route can outpace state fiber programs where regulation permits.
insights.locator: Cambodia recorded an even more dramatic jump

insights.claim: Connectivity expanded in both the Kyrgyz Republic and Cambodia because policy and investment aligned around a single clear national objective of bringing people into the digital economy quickly and at scale, despite using opposite delivery models.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Objective clarity rather than delivery model choice is the common variable, so investors should screen for policy alignment over technology mix.

insights.claim: Ethiopia's national grid reached only a small share of rural communities in 2012, but electricity access has expanded rapidly over the past decade and nearly half of the rural population now has access.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A decade-scale doubling of rural access shows electrification bottlenecks are solvable, which matters for rural productivity and appliance demand forecasts.
insights.locator: Ethiopia advanced by expanding energy access

insights.claim: About three-quarters of Ethiopian rural households gaining electricity access did so through solar power, via off-grid solar home systems and mini-grids rather than grid extension.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Distributed solar, not grid extension, is now the dominant rural electrification channel, favoring off-grid solar and mini-grid operators and financiers over transmission builders.
insights.locator: About three-quarters of rural households gaining access

insights.claim: Ethiopia demonstrates that progress comes from choosing practical solutions that fit local realities rather than waiting for a single perfect model, extending the grid where feasible while deploying off-grid options in remote areas.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Hybrid delivery is the emerging default for electrification programs, which shapes procurement toward mixed portfolios rather than single-technology tenders.
insights.locator: Crucially, Ethiopia did not rely on a single model

themes.theme: Policy implications and the Knowledge Bank

insights.claim: There is no single formula for development: Rwanda advanced through broad-based growth and structural change, the Kyrgyz Republic and Cambodia through digital connectivity, and Ethiopia through pragmatic rural energy, with execution the common factor across all of them.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Argues against template-based development strategy and for judging countries on delivery track record rather than reform blueprints.
insights.locator: They also show that there is no single formula

insights.claim: The World Bank Group is building a Knowledge Bank whose role is to shorten the distance between evidence and implementation, helping countries identify proven approaches, adapt them locally and scale them faster.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Signals an institutional pivot from financing to knowledge intermediation, which affects how the Bank's technical assistance and lending are packaged.
insights.locator: This is precisely why the World Bank Group is building the Knowledge Bank

insights.claim: Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030, is presented as the model of scale required to accelerate development.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A named, dated, quantified target that will drive procurement of generation, distribution and off-grid solar capacity in Africa through 2030.
insights.locator: We need big bets that deliver visible progress

insights.claim: The prescription for policymakers is to prioritize investments that raise productivity, expand access to power and digital infrastructure, strengthen state capacity, and create credible conditions for private investment and job creation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Identifies where development finance is likely to concentrate, with power and digital infrastructure the two named physical priorities.
insights.locator: For policymakers, the message is clear
